title: Drop enough beads at random through rows of pegs and they pile into a bell curve

cover.alt: A wooden Galton board standing upright: a field of pegs above a row of narrow columns, where white beads have piled highest in the middle and lowest at the edges.
cover.credit: Rodrigo.Argenton (video), Estes Objethos Atelier (exhibit) · CC BY-SA 4.0

body: At every peg a bead bounces left or right with equal odds. To reach the far edge it has to bounce the same way at every row, which almost never happens, while a huge number of different routes lead to the middle. The number of routes to each bin follows Pascal’s triangle, so the piles grow into a **binomial distribution**, and with enough rows that looks just like the bell-shaped normal distribution. Francis Galton showed off the board in an 1874 lecture.

slides.alt: A wooden Galton board is tipped upright. A stream of small white beads pours from a funnel through a triangle of pegs and piles up in columns, tallest in the middle and shortest at the edges.
slides.caption: Each bead bounces at random off the pegs, yet the columns build the same bell shape every time: tall in the middle, short at the edges.
slides.credit: Rodrigo.Argenton (video), Estes Objethos Atelier (exhibit), Matemateca IME-USP · CC BY-SA 4.0 · excerpt
slides.music: “Goblin Tinker Soldier Spy” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.question: A board has 10 rows of pegs. Only 1 route leads to each edge bin. How many different routes lead to the middle bin?
slides.explanation: 252: the number of ways to choose which 5 of the 10 bounces go right. So a bead is 252 times more likely to land in the middle than in one edge bin.

slides.heading: Routes to each bin on a board with 5 rows of pegs
slides.note: A row of Pascal’s triangle; with 5 rows of pegs there are 6 bins

slides.text: …the wonderful form of cosmic order expressed by the Law of Frequency of Error.
slides.attribution: Francis Galton, describing the board in Natural Inheritance (1889)

slides.heading: Why the bell keeps appearing
slides.text: Galton made the board to show the central limit theorem. Each bead’s final position is the sum of many small random nudges, left or right. Add up enough independent random nudges and the total tends to follow a bell curve, which is why the shape turns up in so many places.

slides.question: A Galton board has 12 rows of pegs. How many bins does it need at the bottom?
slides.explanation: A board with n rows has n + 1 bins: a bead can bounce right anywhere from 0 to 12 times.
